title: Skreen to Mill Road: Viscosity, Fluorescence, and Fifty-Four Years in Newton's Chair
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Skreen, the rector's youngest son
stops.date_confidence: attested (MacTutor; Wikipedia). The coordinate is corrected: the dossier's 54.25, -8.8567 lands near Templeboy, some 8 km west of the village, which OSM Nominatim puts at 54.2433, -8.7311
stops.campa: In the rectory at Skreen, eleven miles west-southwest of Sligo town, the Rev. Gabriel Stokes and Elizabeth Haughton have their youngest surviving child, the sixth. The house stands within sound of the open Atlantic on a coast so far off the roads that neither coach nor vessel comes near it. The father reads Hebrew and Greek and holds the parish; three of the boy's brothers will take orders after him. Nobody in the house is a mathematician. The child is christened George Gabriel, the second name his father's, and he will sign every paper he publishes with both.
suggested_refs: The glebe house at Skreen, County Sligo, birthplace and childhood home
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
Wikipedia, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Skreen, the coast and the burn
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The burn and the nickname reach this file through family memoir reported in Larmor's 1907 Memoir and are not independently verified; the 1826 date is an ordering device only. The link between this coast and his later subjects is an interpretation, not a documented cause
stops.campa: The boy grows up beside water that never stops moving: breakers on the strand, cloud coming in off the Atlantic, rain crossing the fields in visible sheets. The family remembers a bad burn taken in childhood, and a child who did not cry over it, and an uncle who called him Wellington afterward. He is taught at home and at a school in Sligo. Later writers read the waves and the light of this coast straight into the man who spent his life on the motion of fluids and the change of refrangibility. The parish records say nothing of the kind.
suggested_refs: RTE Brainstorm (28 August 2019), on Stokes and the Sligo coast
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
RTE Brainstorm, 'George Gabriel Stokes' (2019)

stops.name: Hume Street, Dublin: the day boy and the death of the rector
stops.date_confidence: attested for the school, the lodging and the father's death in 1834 (MacTutor); the month is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected: the dossier's 53.3369, -6.2477 falls about 470 m east of the street
stops.campa: At thirteen he is sent to Dublin, to the Rev. R. H. Wall's school in Hume Street, attending as a day boy and lodging with his uncle John Stokes. It is the first time he lives out of hearing of the sea. Two years into it his father dies at Skreen and the living passes to another man, so the rectory stops being a place he can go back to. What is paid for after that is arranged among an uncle and older brothers, none of whom is rich. He stays in Dublin three years altogether.
suggested_refs: Hume Street, Dublin 2, site of R. H. Wall's school
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Waterford quay, the packet Killarney
stops.date_confidence: the 1835 move to Bristol is attested (MacTutor); the near-foundering and the greatcoat are family recollection from his brother William, reconstruction only. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: He goes down to Waterford to take the packet Killarney for Bristol. Mid-passage the vessel nearly founders, and his brother William will remember afterward what the boy of sixteen did about it: took off his greatcoat and folded it, so as to be ready to swim. It is the same story the family tells about the childhood burn, told again with more water in it: a boy who does the practical thing and makes no noise about it. The ship makes Bristol, and Bristol College takes him in the autumn of 1835. He is sixteen years old.
suggested_refs: The Waterford to Bristol packet service of the 1830s
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
Family recollection of William Stokes via secondary biographical summaries

stops.name: Bristol College, Park Street
stops.date_confidence: attested for the college and the 1835-1837 dates (MacTutor); the teachers' names and the January 1837 prize come from memoir tradition and were not reverified. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: Two years at Bristol College under the principal Joseph Henry Jerrard, with Francis William Newman among the teachers, brother to the John Henry Newman then unsettling Oxford. In January 1837 he takes the college mathematics prize. Jerrard, who thinks he knows what the boy is, urges the family to send him to Trinity College, Cambridge, the largest and richest foundation in the university. The family sends him to Pembroke instead, a smaller and older foundation with no particular name in mathematics, where a fellowship might actually fall to him.
suggested_refs: Bristol College, Park Street, 1831-1841
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Pembroke College, matriculation without the calculus
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1837 matriculation and for his own account of arriving without the differential calculus (MacTutor, quoting the autobiographical note printed in Larmor); the month is an ordering device
stops.campa: He comes up to Pembroke at eighteen and arrives, by his own later account, without having begun the differential calculus, less far along than the college's advertised course implies. The Tripos is a four-year forced march toward one ranked examination in the Senate House, and every man in it knows his number will follow him for life. Stokes reads. He joins no society and leaves behind, out of these first years, no anecdotes at all: only a record of what he read and how far he got with it.
stops.quote: In those days boys coming to the University had not in general read so far in mathematics as is the custom at present...
stops.quote_source: Stokes's own autobiographical account, printed in Larmor's Memoir (1907), quoted on MacTutor
suggested_refs: Pembroke College, Cambridge, his college from 1837 until his death
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Cambridge, reading with Hopkins
stops.date_confidence: attested for the coaching, in Stokes's own words on MacTutor; the framing of Hopkins's teaching as the finding of order in nature is secondary tradition. The Venables letter naming Cayley is dated summer 1842 and is carried in arthur_cayley.journey.json
stops.campa: In his second year he begins reading with William Hopkins, the private coach the university calls the Senior Wrangler maker, who takes a fee and a small number of men and drills them through the whole apparatus. Hopkins does not teach mathematics as a set of examination tricks. He teaches astronomy and optics as the finding of order in the world, and he pushes Stokes toward hydrodynamics, which nobody in England is working. Arthur Cayley is in the same stable at Trinity, a year behind, and will turn up in Stokes's own post within a few years as the butt of a mathematical joke about weighing the earth.
stops.quote: In my second year I began to read with a private tutor, Mr Hopkins, who was celebrated for the very large number of his pupils gaining high places in the University examinations...
stops.quote_source: Stokes's own autobiographical account, quoted on MacTutor
suggested_refs: William Hopkins's coaching practice at Cambridge, 1830s-1850s
Venables to Stokes, summer 1842, on Cayley and Schiehallion
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Senate House, Senior Wrangler
stops.date_confidence: attested (MacTutor; Wikipedia). The pin is inherited byte-identical from arthur_cayley.journey.json, 'Cambridge Senate House: Senior Wrangler'
stops.campa: In January the lists are read out in the Senate House and Stokes stands at the head of them: Senior Wrangler, and first Smith's Prizeman as well, the double that settles a career in one morning. Pembroke elects him to a fellowship at once, four years after taking him in without the calculus. He is twenty-one years old. Cayley will take the same double the following January. In the autumn a Glasgow boy of seventeen named William Thomson comes up to Peterhouse, already reading Fourier and Laplace.

stops.name: Pembroke College, the first paper
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the paper and the year (MacTutor); the exact date of the reading comes from the standard bibliographic record and was not reverified in any pass
stops.campa: He stays in college, takes private pupils as Hopkins did before him, and reads to the Cambridge Philosophical Society a paper called On the Steady Motion of Incompressible Fluids. It is his first. The subject is water, and air, and anything that flows, treated as a continuum with equations attached. Papers on a piston and the air in a cylinder follow, then viscous flow. The Continental analysts he is answering, Navier and Poisson and Cauchy and Saint-Venant, are barely read in England, and he is working through them alone in a set of college rooms.
stops.quote: After taking my degree I continued to reside in College and took private pupils. I thought I would try my hand at original research....
stops.quote_source: Stokes's own autobiographical account, quoted on MacTutor
suggested_refs: Transactions of the Cambridge Philosophical Society, vol. 7 (1842)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Cambridge, the internal friction of fluids
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1845 paper (MacTutor) and for the 1846 British Association report (MacTutor). The pool names no meeting city for 1846, so the report is carried here, where it was written, rather than at a guessed venue. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: He publishes On the Theories of the Internal Friction of Fluids in Motion, and of the Equilibrium and Motion of Elastic Solids. Navier had begun the thing in 1822 and Poisson had derived it independently; what Stokes does is put it into the form that holds. Friction inside the fluid itself, the stickiness of water against water, enters the equations of motion and stays there. The next year he reports to the British Association on recent researches in hydrodynamics, a survey of the whole field as it then stood.
suggested_refs: Stokes, 'On the Theories of the Internal Friction of Fluids in Motion' (1845)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
Wikipedia, 'Navier-Stokes equations'

stops.name: Cambridge, Newton's chair and the falling sphere
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1849 election and for Stokes's law in 1851 (MacTutor); the month is an ordering device
stops.campa: At thirty he is elected Lucasian Professor of Mathematics, the chair Isaac Barrow stood down from in 1669 to hand to Newton. It is a famous chair and a poor one; the endowment will not keep a household, and Stokes takes physics teaching in London to make up the difference. Two years into it he publishes the law of the drag on a small sphere moving through a viscous fluid, which is why a fog droplet falls slowly and a stone does not. He will hold this chair for fifty-four years.
suggested_refs: Stokes, 'On the Effect of the Internal Friction of Fluids on the Motion of Pendulums' (1851)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Belfast, two hours of sunlight through quinine
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1852 British Association met at Belfast (Wikipedia, list of meetings) and that Stokes named and explained fluorescence and took the Rumford Medal in 1852 (MacTutor); the hall within Belfast is not attested and is not named here
stops.campa: He has found that a solution of quinine, lit by the invisible radiation past the violet end of the spectrum, gives back light of lower refrangibility, visible blue. He gives the thing a name, fluorescence, after the fluorspar in which it was first noticed. At the British Association in Belfast he stands for two hours with sunlight, prisms, quinine and chlorophyll, turning invisible light into visible light in front of a public audience. The Royal Society gives him the Rumford Medal that year. He is thirty-three.
suggested_refs: Stokes, 'On the Change of Refrangibility of Light' (1852)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
Wikipedia, 'List of British Science Association annual meetings'

stops.name: Cambridge, a theorem set as an examination question
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Both halves of this story, the July 1850 letter from Thomson and the 1854 Smith's Prize question, reach this file through dossier synthesis of Larmor's edited Stokes-Thomson correspondence and of Cambridge examination records, neither of which was fetched directly in any pass. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: William Thomson had sent him, in a letter four years earlier, the identity between a line integral taken round a closed curve and a surface integral over any surface that curve bounds. Stokes does not publish it and does not claim it. He sets it as a question on the Smith's Prize paper, where every candidate for the prize has to prove it, and that is where the name attaches: the students call it Stokes's theorem because Stokes is the man who asked them for it. He never claimed it as his own.
suggested_refs: The Smith's Prize examination paper, Cambridge, 1854

segments.name: The Society and the School of Mines

stops.name: Somerset House, the Strand: elected Fellow
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1851 election and the 1854 secretaryship (MacTutor); the month is an ordering device. The Royal Society occupied Somerset House until the 1850s and Burlington House thereafter, so the election and the long secretaryship belong to two different buildings, which the dossier had merged
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects him a Fellow. He is thirty-one, three years into the Lucasian chair, and he comes into the Society's rooms with a finished field behind him rather than a promising one. Three years later the Fellows make him one of the two secretaries. The Society moves west while he holds the post, out of the Strand and up to Piccadilly, and he goes with it. He is one of the two secretaries from 1854 until 1885, thirty-one years in the same office.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society's apartments at Somerset House, 1780-1852
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
Wikipedia, 'Royal Society'

stops.name: Jermyn Street, the School of Mines
stops.date_confidence: contradiction in the pool, not resolved: the chronology dates the appointment 1857, the geography dates the London teaching circa 1854-1859, and MacTutor has him resigning in 1859 when Cambridge improved the Lucasian endowment. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: The Lucasian chair does not pay enough to keep a household, so he takes the professorship of physics at the Government School of Mines in Jermyn Street and splits his residence between two cities, lecturing to men who will go out to survey coal and ore. He is Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge and a jobbing physics lecturer in London in the same week. In 1859 the university raises the endowment and he gives the London post up. Nothing in the correspondence complains about the arrangement.
suggested_refs: The Government School of Mines, Jermyn Street, London
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Burlington House, the secretary's desk
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was a secretary of the Royal Society from 1854 to 1885 (MacTutor) and that the Society occupied Burlington House from 1857 (Wikipedia). The Maxwell correspondence on optics, colour vision and publication reaches this file through the dossier alone and is not carried in james_clerk_maxwell.journey.json; it is reconstruction. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: For thirty-one years every paper submitted to the Royal Society crosses his desk. He reads them, refers them, writes to the authors, and sends work back with objections that are usually right and always civil. Stokes publishes less under his own name in these decades than he did in the 1840s, and a great deal of his work goes unsigned into other men's papers. James Clerk Maxwell, twelve years younger, sends him optics and colour vision, and gets back the kind of reply that changes a paper before it is printed.
suggested_refs: The Royal Society archives, secretary's correspondence 1854-1885
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'
Wikipedia, 'Royal Society'

stops.name: Pittville Pump Room, Cheltenham
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1856 British Association met at Cheltenham and that Stokes first met Mary Susanna Robinson at a meeting that year; the Pump Room as the specific venue is the researcher's inference, stated in neither source, and the exact August date is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected to the Nominatim value
stops.campa: At the British Association meeting he is introduced to Mary Susanna Robinson, only daughter of Thomas Romney Robinson, who directs the observatory at Armagh. He takes her for some while to be a daughter of Sir David Brewster, and afterward has real difficulty working out which young woman he has been talking to. He is thirty-six years old and has spent nineteen of them in a college of unmarried men, reading. There is nothing in the record to suggest he has done this before.
suggested_refs: The 26th meeting of the British Association, Cheltenham, 1856

stops.name: Birr Castle, the tube of the great telescope
stops.date_confidence: attested that Stokes advised the Earl of Rosse on the telescope's optics (RTE Brainstorm) and that the courtship proceeded partly within the Rosse circle (skullsinthestars). The proposal legend is family tradition, called absolute fiction by Stokes's own daughter Isabella; the passage could not be relocated in the archive.org scan. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: William Parsons, third Earl of Rosse, keeps at Birr the largest telescope on earth, a six-foot mirror slung in a tube between two masonry walls, and around it a circle of people who come to look through it. Stokes advises on its optics. Mary is in the same circle. The story the family tells afterward is that he proposed to her inside the tube, in the dark, with the sky at the far end of it. His daughter Isabella writes the story down and calls it absolute fiction in the same sentence.
suggested_refs: The Leviathan of Parsonstown, Birr Castle, County Offaly

stops.name: Armagh Observatory, the winter letters
stops.date_confidence: attested as the observatory Mary's father directed and as the household in which the courtship partly proceeded; the letters are printed in Larmor's Memoir (1907) and reach this file through skullsinthestars.com, wording not checked against page images. The thinking machine phrase is memoir tradition
stops.campa: The courtship runs by post between Cambridge and the observatory at Armagh, and the letters are strange ones. He writes about religion, about whether he is fit to marry at all, about his own coldness. He tells her she should draw back rather than go on unwilling, even if it returns him to life as a thinking machine. One letter runs to fifty-five pages. He also reports the state of his health to her in the only vocabulary he entirely trusts. She keeps them all.
stops.quote: My cold is gone, reduced to only the dregs of the dregs of a cold, an infinitesimal of the second order.
stops.quote_source: Stokes to Mary Susanna Robinson, 10 January 1857, in Larmor, Memoir and Scientific Correspondence (1907)

stops.name: St Patrick's Cathedral, Armagh: the marriage and the fellowship
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia; MacTutor). Coordinate corrected: Nominatim gives St Patrick's Cathedral, Vicars Hill, Armagh at 54.3478, -6.6562, about 230 m southwest of the dossier's point
stops.campa: They are married in the cathedral on the hill at Armagh, her father's city. Pembroke's statutes at that date permit no married fellow, so the fellowship he won at twenty-one goes the moment the words are said and he is left holding only the chair. He is thirty-seven. The bride's father has spent his life on a telescope and the groom has spent his on light, and nobody at the wedding finds the match odd. Five years later the college revises the statute and elects him back.
stops.quote: I feel that perhaps my marriage with you would be even the turning-point of my salvation.
stops.quote_source: Stokes to Mary Susanna Robinson, 1857, quoted on MacTutor from the letters printed in Larmor's Memoir
suggested_refs: St Patrick's Cathedral (Church of Ireland), Vicars Hill, Armagh

stops.name: The Rigi, quartz prisms on the honeymoon
stops.date_confidence: attested from his letter of 11 May 1857, which names both the Rigi and the Faulhorn as sites for the observations (skullsinthestars, quoting Larmor); the August date is an ordering device
stops.campa: Before the wedding he writes to her about the luggage. Switzerland has thin air and high sun, which means more of the invisible radiation past the violet reaches the ground there than ever reaches Cambridge, and quartz will pass that radiation where ordinary glass stops it. So the honeymoon carries two quartz prisms, a quartz lens and a piece of uranium glass up the Rigi. He is proposing to examine the solar spectrum from the top of a mountain with his wife of three weeks standing next to him.
stops.quote: If we are married at the time we are at present thinking of, and go to Switzerland...I think I will bring a couple of quartz prisms, a quartz lens, and a piece of uranium glass with me.
stops.quote_source: Stokes to Mary Susanna Robinson, 11 May 1857, in Larmor, Memoir and Scientific Correspondence (1907); ellipsis present in the source
suggested_refs: The Rigi, Canton Schwyz, named in the letter of 11 May 1857
sources: skullsinthestars.com, 'George Gabriel Stokes in Love (1857)'

stops.name: The Faulhorn, the journal Mary keeps
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Faulhorn was named in the 11 May letter as a site for the observations; the journal line is verified at primary level in Larmor vol. 1, where the OCR reads waterspots. It is her journal of the Swiss honeymoon, not a diary in general. The August date is an ordering device. Coordinate corrected to the Wikipedia and Nominatim summit position
stops.campa: The second summit on the list. She is keeping a journal, and what goes into it is not the spectrum. It is her husband in the mountains: delighted by storms, walking deliberately under every waterspout on the path, up and down all day in the wet. The man who wrote her fifty-five pages on whether he was fit to marry is, on a Swiss hillside three weeks in, putting his head under falling water for the pleasure of it. He is thirty-seven years old. The prisms do not get into the journal at all.
stops.quote: George is so fond of lightning. He puts his head under all the waterspouts he can find.
stops.quote_source: Mary Susanna Stokes's journal of the Swiss honeymoon, 1857, in Larmor, Memoir and Scientific Correspondence, vol. 1

stops.name: Lensfield Cottage, the house he does not leave
stops.date_confidence: attested as his home from 1857 until his death (Wikipedia) and for the 1862 re-election to the Pembroke fellowship under revised statutes (MacTutor); the month is an ordering device
stops.campa: They settle at Lensfield, on the southern edge of Cambridge, in a cottage that gets enlarged around them across forty-five years without ever quite ceasing to be a cottage. Children are born here and two of them die young. In 1862 Pembroke revises the statute that cost him the fellowship and elects him back to it, so that he holds fellowship and chair together again as he did at twenty-one. He stays at Lensfield forty-five years and dies there in 1903.

segments.name: Light, Blood, and Credit Not Claimed

stops.name: Cambridge, the credit he does not claim
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The priority episode, and Thomson's insistence that Stokes had taught him spectral identification orally before the summer of 1852, reach this file through dossier synthesis of the Stokes-Thomson correspondence and were not confirmed against primary correspondence in any pass. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: Kirchhoff and Bunsen publish spectrum analysis out of Heidelberg: every element carries its own set of lines, and a spectrum will tell you what a thing is made of, a star included. William Thomson says, then and for the rest of his life, that Stokes had explained the principle to him in conversation before the summer of 1852 and ought to have the credit for it. Stokes never says it himself, and no paper of his has been found that makes the claim. The credit stands where the printed papers put it, with Kirchhoff and Bunsen.
suggested_refs: The Kirchhoff-Bunsen spectroscopy papers, 1859-1860
sources: Dossier synthesis of the Stokes-Thomson correspondence and the priority episode, not independently confirmed
lord_kelvin.journey.json

stops.name: Cambridge, the colour of blood
stops.date_confidence: the paper and its result are attested, but the pool reaches them through dossier synthesis of Stokes's published papers rather than a fetched source; the month is an ordering device
stops.campa: He turns the spectroscope on blood and finds that the colouring matter has two spectra and not one: a two-banded absorption when it is carrying oxygen, a single broader band when it has given the oxygen up. Reduction and oxidation, made visible as a change in light. A physicist working on his own at Lensfield hands physiology a method for telling whether blood is carrying air, which is the thing blood is for. The paper is called On the Reduction and Oxidation of the Colouring Matter of the Blood.
suggested_refs: Stokes, 'On the Reduction and Oxidation of the Colouring Matter of the Blood' (1864)
sources: Dossier synthesis of Stokes's published papers, not independently fetched

stops.name: Exeter, president of the British Association
stops.date_confidence: attested that the 1869 meeting was at Exeter (Wikipedia) and that Stokes presided over it (MacTutor); the venue within Exeter is not reverified and the August date is an ordering device
stops.campa: Seventeen years after standing up in Belfast with a prism and a glass of quinine, he takes the chair of the whole Association at Exeter and gives the presidential address. The Association is at this date the largest public forum science has in Britain, a week of sections and evening lectures moving to a different city every summer. He is fifty years old, seventeen years past the two hours with the quinine and the prisms, and he did not stand for the office.
suggested_refs: The 39th meeting of the British Association, Exeter, 1869
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes'

stops.name: Rathmines, Dublin: Grubb's optical works
stops.date_confidence: the consultation with Howard Grubb at Rathmines is stated flatly by RTE Brainstorm with no date given at all, and no second source was found in any pass. The 1875 date is an ordering device and nothing more
stops.campa: Back in Dublin, at the optical works in Rathmines, Howard Grubb grinds and mounts the object glasses that go out to observatories from Vienna to Melbourne. Stokes comes and consults with him. The theory of aberration and the actual figuring of a large lens are two different trades, and Stokes has spent his life inside both: the man who wrote the equations for viscous drag also tells telescope builders what curve to cut. No source reached in any pass of this research says what year this was.
suggested_refs: Howard Grubb's optical works, Rathmines, Dublin
sources: RTE Brainstorm, 'George Gabriel Stokes' (2019)

stops.name: Westminster, the wind on the Tay
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Board of Trade Court of Inquiry held its engineering sessions at Westminster from 19 April to 8 May 1880 and Stokes testified there on wind loading (Wikipedia, 'Tay Bridge disaster'). The dossier chronology had dated this 1879, the year of the disaster itself, which is wrong
stops.campa: On the night of 28 December 1879 the high girders of the Tay Bridge went into the river in a gale with a train inside them. The Board of Trade inquiry sits at Westminster through the spring, and Stokes is called on wind pressure: how gusts behave, how they are measured, what correction a gauge needs before its reading means anything. He tells the court that a catspaw on open water, one of those dark patches of wind crossing a surface, can run hundreds of yards across it. The bridge had been built to a wind figure nobody had tested.
suggested_refs: Report of the Court of Inquiry into the Tay Bridge disaster, 1880
sources: Wikipedia, 'Tay Bridge disaster'

stops.name: Marischal College, Aberdeen: the Burnett Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested that Stokes was Burnett Lecturer at Aberdeen for three courses across 1883-1885, published as On Light (DNB 1912 supplement). MacTutor dates the Burnett lectures 1891-93, conflating them with the Gifford lectures at Edinburgh; the DNB separation is followed here. Marischal College as the specific venue is not reverified. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: Three winters of lectures at Aberdeen on the Burnett foundation, published afterward as a book called On Light. He takes light from the beginning: what it is, how the eye receives it, what the spectrum is doing, and then what an examined world implies about the one who made it, because the Burnett bequest was set up to have exactly that argued from the platform. The physics and the natural theology go into the same volume, and he does not hedge either half of it.
suggested_refs: Stokes, On Light: Burnett Lectures delivered at Aberdeen, 1883-1885
sources: Dictionary of National Biography, 1912 supplement, 'Stokes, Sir George Gabriel'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'George Gabriel Stokes' (conflicting dates, flagged)

stops.name: Burlington House, President of the Royal Society
stops.date_confidence: attested that he succeeded T. H. Huxley as President and served to 1890, and that he worried in writing about giving up the secretary's salary (Wikipedia; MacTutor). The exact November date is the Society's anniversary day and is used as an ordering device
stops.campa: He succeeds Thomas Henry Huxley in the president's chair, having sat as secretary in the same building since Huxley was a young man. He worries about it in writing first, because the president draws no salary where the secretary did, and there is still a family to keep; the improved Lucasian endowment is what makes it possible to accept. He is sixty-six years old and has been a secretary of the Society since 1854. He will hold the presidency five years, to 1890.

A heritable honour of the British state is attached by its own wording to a cottage on the south edge of Cambridge that he moved into as a married man of thirty-seven and has never once left. stops.name: Old College, Edinburgh: the Gifford Lectures
stops.date_confidence: attested that he gave the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh in 1891 and 1893, published as Natural Theology (giffordlectures.org), and that he was president of the Victoria Institute from 1886 until his death (Wikipedia). The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: Adam Gifford's will endows lectures on natural theology treated as a strict science, and Edinburgh gives two courses of them to Stokes. He argues from order and design, defends providence, and holds that a human being is not exhausted by the account physics can give of a body. He is the sitting President of the Royal Society while he says it, and he says it in the decade in which the argument is losing. He is also president of the Victoria Institute, founded to discuss Christianity in relation to contemporary science, and remains so until he dies.

stops.name: Pembroke College garden, fifty years in the chair

stops.campa: Fifty years to the year since his election to the Lucasian chair, and Cambridge holds an international jubilee for it. Delegations arrive from academies across Europe, North America and the Empire with addresses to read out. William Thomson, now Lord Kelvin, who has been writing to him since they were both young men in this town, is the moving force behind the whole thing. The party is held in the garden at Pembroke. Marble busts by Hamo Thornycroft are presented to the college and the university, and the French Academy sends the Arago medal.

He sits down in its hall as the senior mathematician in Britain, holding the chair Newton held, with a gold portrait medal from the university in his hand. He is seventy-nine. Almost everything the addresses celebrate was finished before he was forty-five. He has seven months left in which his wife is alive.

stops.date_confidence: attested for the date (Wikipedia); the location at the family home is inferred and is not stated in the fetched source
stops.campa: Mary Susanna Stokes dies at the end of December, six months after the garden party. She had come from an observatory in Armagh to a cottage in Cambridge forty-two years earlier, kept the journal of the honeymoon, and read every one of the letters in which he asked whether he was fit to marry her. He does not marry again and he does not leave the house; he is eighty and has three years to run. She is buried at Mill Road, in a grave with room beside it.

stops.name: Pembroke College, elected Master
stops.date_confidence: the pool contradicts itself and both of its dates are wrong. The chronology gives 12 August 1902 and calls it the last day of his eighty-third year; the geography gives 31 December 1902. DNB 1912 says October 1902; the Times obituary says he agreed to nomination in August, on the death of Master Searle; French Wikipedia gives 26 August 1902. His eighty-third birthday fell on 13 August 1902. The date here is an ordering device inside the attested August to October window
stops.campa: Dr Searle, Master of Pembroke, dies in the August, and the fellows ask Stokes to let his name go forward. He agrees, and they elect him. He is eighty-three and in his fifty-fourth year as Lucasian Professor, and he now heads the college that took him in at eighteen without the calculus, put him out at thirty-seven for marrying, and took him back at forty-two. He holds the mastership and the Lucasian chair together, and goes on living alone at Lensfield, at the other end of the town from the college he now heads.

stops.campa: He has been visibly failing for months. The family record says the mind stays clear almost to the end, that there is a short delirium in which he believes he is addressing undergraduates, and that the death itself is quiet. He dies at home, eighty-three years old, Master of Pembroke and Lucasian Professor of fifty-four years, in the house whose name is written into his title. It is fifty-four years since the election to the chair and sixty-one since he arrived at Pembroke without the calculus. The Times has the obituary out within two days.

stops.name: Cambridge, five volumes and a memoir
stops.date_confidence: attested: the first three volumes of the Mathematical and Physical Papers were selected by Stokes himself (1880, 1883, 1891) and the last two completed by Joseph Larmor by 1905; Larmor edited the two-volume Memoir and Scientific Correspondence in 1907, with the personal section written by Stokes's daughter Isabella Lucy Humphry. The Stokes Society was founded at Pembroke in 1909. The month is an ordering device
stops.campa: Joseph Larmor finishes what Stokes began: the last two volumes of the Mathematical and Physical Papers, and then two volumes of memoir and correspondence, into which Stokes's daughter Isabella Lucy Humphry writes the life. That is how the courtship letters reach print, the fifty-five pages and the dregs of the dregs of a cold and the proposal in the telescope tube that she herself calls fiction. Two years after that, the undergraduates of Pembroke found a scientific society and put his name on it.

stops.name: Dublin City University, the name on a building
stops.date_confidence: attested that Dublin City University named a building after Stokes in July 2017 (Wikipedia). The wider question of Irish versus British possession of Stokes is raised in the dossier and is not adjudicated here. The day is an ordering device
stops.campa: A university in Dublin puts his name on a building. He was born in a Sligo rectory, schooled in Hume Street, sailed out of Waterford at sixteen, courted a wife in Armagh and advised a telescope maker in Rathmines, and then spent sixty-six working years in England holding English offices and taking English honours. Which country he belongs to has never been settled. Both answers are built from that same list of places, and no source reached here proposes a way to choose between them.

stops.name: Pembroke College, Stokes at two hundred
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Stokes 200 symposium ran at Pembroke College from 15 to 18 September 2019, co-organised by Silvana Cardoso, Julyan Cartwright and Christopher Ness (Pembroke College). The resulting Philosophical Transactions A theme issue appeared in 2020, not 2019, per the DOI resolution; the Royal Society's own site returned 403 to this research
stops.campa: Two hundred years after the rectory at Skreen, mathematicians and fluid dynamicists sit for four days in Pembroke and read papers about him. The equations he put into their final form in 1845 are still open: whether smooth solutions exist in three dimensions for all time is one of the seven Clay Millennium Prize Problems, a million dollars against a proof nobody has. Water goes on doing it in the meantime, unproved. The theme issue that comes out of the meeting is published the following year.
